generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport you paraphrase far more often than you quote, because what usually matters is a study's finding or a policy's implication, not an author's exact wording. That makes paraphrase the place where integrity is most often tested. A sound paraphrase of a result or a participation figure rebuilds it in your own words and still cites the source. A paraphrase that keeps the original's distinctive phrasing, even with a citation, shows the words were moved rather than the finding understood.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport management and development students want to use the same sentence from a report on a participation campaign.

Tom decides to paraphrase, but stays close to the original: a few words are swapped for synonyms while the sentence keeps its shape and its distinctive phrasing. A citation is added, so it feels above board. Yet the expression is still the report's, not Tom's. Cited or not, this patchwriting shows the words were moved, not the finding understood.

Amara judges that the report's exact wording is not what matters here, only its finding about participation, so paraphrase is the right move. She sets the source aside, writes the point from memory in her own words, then checks back to confirm the meaning holds and the wording is genuinely hers. The source is cited. The paraphrase shows understanding, because it is rebuilt rather than relabelled.

Both cited the source. Only Amara made a judgement about how to use it that kept the integrity intact.
generatedProse.summary: Using a source well in the School of Sport is a matter of judgement. You quote when the exact wording matters, such as a precise policy definition, and paraphrase, the more common move, when you want the finding in your own voice. A sound paraphrase rebuilds the idea in genuinely new words and still cites the source; one that only swaps a few words stays the source's expression and fails even when cited. You can now judge between quoting and paraphrasing, tell a sound paraphrase from one too close to the source, and decide how to handle a report or study so its integrity holds. With the values, the reasons and the judgement in place, referencing is something you can own and defend.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Tom's paraphrase fail even though it was cited?

items.text: It kept the source's shape and phrasing with only a few words swapped, so the expression was still the source's.
It paraphrased a finding that should have been quoted directly instead.
It cited the wrong report for the sentence being used.
It was shorter than the original sentence from the report.

feedback.correct: That's right. Patchwriting keeps the source's expression, and a citation does not make it the student's own work.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about whose words the paragraph really contained, citation aside.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The paraphrase failed because it kept the source's shape and phrasing with only words swapped, so the expression was still the source's. A citation cannot make lifted expression your own work.
